entities.name: Muhammad XII of Granada
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Abu Abdallah Muhammad XII, known to Castilians as Boabdil, reigned as the 22nd and final Nasrid Sultan of Granada from 1487 to 1492, though his rule was punctuated by earlier periods of deposition and restoration. His reign culminated in the surrender of Granada on January 2, 1492, to the Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile, marking the definitive end of nearly eight centuries of Muslim rule on the Iberian Peninsula and concluding the Christian Reconquista. His personal tragedy and political misfortunes became emblematic of the twilight of Al-Andalus, fundamentally reshaping the political and cultural landscape of Western Europe and contributing to the formation of modern Spain.

Muhammad XII's ascent to power was marred by dynastic conflicts, famously imprisoning his own father, Abu al-Hasan Ali, and later warring with his uncle, al-Zagal, for control of the fragmented emirate. This internal disunity critically weakened Granada as the Catholic Monarchs systematically absorbed the surrounding Nasrid territories. After his capture by Castilian forces at Lucena in 1483, Muhammad XII was briefly released under terms that made him a tributary vassal, further eroding Granada's sovereignty. The pivotal event was the protracted Siege of Granada, beginning in April 1491, which saw the construction of Santa Fe by the Castilian army, demonstrating their unyielding resolve.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Muhammad XII's rule culminated in the fall of Granada in 1492, ending nearly 800 years of Muslim presence in Iberia and completing the Reconquista, which was a pivotal event in the formation of modern Spain and the expansion of Christian European power.
